title: Rerum Novarum again (1891)
hookLine: a worker signs for a wage too low to live on: is the deal fair because it was agreed?

cards: A worker needs a job, and there's no other job in sight. The owner offers a wage too small to live on, and the worker signs. Hands are shaken.
Nobody was forced at gunpoint. So is that wage fair, simply because both sides agreed to it? Plenty of arguments say a deal is a deal.
Leo's letter, the one this block opened with, says something else; its closing line says it was given at Rome in 1891. Today, a just wage.

teach.b: First, Leo's answer. When a worker accepts harder terms because necessity, or fear of something worse, leaves no choice, he writes, the worker is the victim of force and injustice.
A signature made with no real alternative doesn't make a wage just. Second, the measure.
A wage, Leo says, must be enough to support a worker who lives frugally and behaves well.

And he hopes for more: a wage that lets a worker support a wife and children in reasonable comfort, and still put a little aside, so that over time ordinary workers might come to own something themselves.
Sending out disciples in Luke, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "the labourer is worthy of his hire." The Greek word for hire there is misthos, wages.

And the letter of James warns the rich that the wages held back from the workers who reaped their fields cry out, and that the cry reaches the ears of the Lord. Leo's letter stands in that line. Fourth, what it means now.
The Catechism calls a just wage the legitimate fruit of work, and says that refusing or withholding it can be a grave injustice. Today people speak of a living wage, close to what Leo described.
What counts as enough changes with the place and the prices. The principle stays put: in this teaching, honest work should pay enough to live on and to raise a family.

how: Catholic bishops and organizations cite Rerum Novarum in debates about minimum and living wages, and Catholic employers are urged by Church teaching to pay wages that let workers support a family.

games.q: you're a worker with no other job in sight. the owner offers a wage too low to live on, and you sign. in Leo's letter, is that wage now just?
o: no: a deal made out of necessity doesn't make it just.
only if the owner is losing money.
games.why: Leo writes that a worker forced by necessity or fear to accept harder terms is the victim of force and injustice.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose work your day depends on: the person who stocks the shelves, the aide at a care home, the cook.

Ask, without rushing to an answer, what a household in your town needs for rent, food and the basics, and whether their pay could support a family here. Just hold the question; if you pray, you can pray for them.

wordCard.voice: Just wage. In Leo's letter, a wage enough for a worker to live on and support a family, and not made just merely because it was agreed. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: wages, hire. the word behind hire in Luke's worthy of his hire.

carryVoice: Your line: a just wage. A deal alone doesn't make it fair. One thousand three hundred days now.
